name: bulk_extractor
why: A stream-based forensics scanner that carves emails, URLs and card numbers out of raw disk images, revealing what hides in bytes.

brief.what_it_is: bulk_extractor is a command-line digital forensics tool that scans disk images, individual files, or directories of files and pulls out structured evidence such as email addresses, credit card numbers, JPEGs and JSON snippets. It does not parse the file system. Results are written as text files that can be searched or fed into other forensic tools, and it also builds histograms of features it finds, such as email addresses and Google search terms. The repo describes it as a "get evidence" button for any kind of input. The Windows section also says it can read a raw physical disk or volume by device path.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a fast way to triage large amounts of data without depending on file-system structure, and says histograms of features like search terms and email addresses have proven useful in investigative and law enforcement work. The citation points to Garfinkel's 2013 paper "Digital media triage with bulk data analysis and bulk_extractor".
brief.how_it_works: It probes every byte of input to see whether it starts a sequence that can be decompressed or decoded, such as Base64 or compressed data. Anything decoded is recursively re-scanned, which is how it finds things like Base64-encoded JPEGs and compressed JSON that traditional carvers miss. It runs stream-based scanners over the data, and scanner modules can be loaded as scan_*.so, .dylib or .dll plugins from directories given with -P or in BE_PATH.

brief.install_notes: Build from source: git clone, then ./bootstrap.sh, ./configure, make, make check, make install. The README says the source tree builds 2.2.0 and recommends a tagged release from the GitHub releases page for production use. It requires C++17. Setup scripts in etc/ are described as possibly needing maintenance. Full install instructions are in doc/installation.md in the repo. Native Windows builds are not supported; the only Windows option is a cross-compiled, unsigned CI artifact built on Ubuntu with MinGW. A Docker image (Debian Bookworm, runs unprivileged) is provided for scanning regular image files, but it leaves out libewf and Lightgrep. Homebrew is the install path named in the brief, but no Homebrew-specific notes appeared in the README.
brief.standout: Its optimistic decoding is the distinctive part: it checks every byte for the start of encoded or compressed data and re-scans whatever it decodes, instead of relying on file headers or the file system. Output is plain text and histograms meant for downstream analysis, and loadable scanner plugins are supported.
brief.status: Maintained. The README says the 2.2.0 release is dated August 17, 2026, and the 2.1.1 release is dated April 26, 2024. The validation note is dated 2026-07-19. The wiki's Home page was last edited August 6, 2026 and now mostly points to the in-tree docs.
brief.caveats: Native Windows builds are not supported; only an unsigned cross-compiled CI artifact is available. Debian 10 is listed as unsupported. Tested configurations are Apple Silicon macOS and Ubuntu 22.04 and current macOS GitHub runners. The Docker image is not a privileged raw-device appliance and omits libewf and Lightgrep. The wiki is now only a navigation layer, and the README says it is not authoritative for current releases. The scout note's list of URLs is not in the README; it names emails, credit card numbers, JPEGs and JSON. The README says the source tree is not the same as a tested release.
